about: Round 2 of the one-pager: the owner's 2025 nicotine one-pager rebuilt as a template for eight addictions. Ref keys are the research item's own ids (r1, r2...) or ids in globalRefs. Every belief, milestone and number points at a ref already fetched in files 01-04, except where a ref there says fetched: false (shown as unchecked).
plan: Identify what beliefs are driving your {thing}. Find a positive reframe (the table below).
Find “80%” alternatives: if you think {thing} relaxes you, find something that meets 80% of that need, like reading, a show, or talking to a friend.
Set a date (some days or weeks ahead) and make this the one thing for the next three months. Every day you keep that promise to yourself is a complete success. If you slip, go back through steps 1–3.
From that day on, act, think and feel as if you have already quit. Ask yourself: “why would I {verb}, when I’ve been {free} for a year already and I enjoy my life so much more now?”
Get help (optional): friends, family, therapy, rehab, 12-step groups, or 1-on-1 help from me.

globalRefs.cite: Lopez-Quintero C, Hasin DS, de los Cobos JP, et al. (2011). Probability and predictors of remission from life-time nicotine, alcohol, cannabis or cocaine dependence: results from NESARC. Addiction.
globalRefs.supports: Lifetime remission 83.7% nicotine, 90.6% alcohol, 97.2% cannabis, 99.2% cocaine; half remitted about 26, 14, 6 and 5 years after onset. Abstract re-fetched 2026-11-04.

pages.title: Quitting alcohol

hero.line: of people ever hooked on alcohol are expected to get free of it in their lifetime.
hero.sub: Half took about 14 years. You don’t have to wait that long.
hero.basedOn: A US survey of 43,093 adults in 2001–02. 4,781 of them had ever been hooked on alcohol. From the age each one got free, a standard statistical model projects the share over a whole life.
hero.caveat: “Free” means no signs of being hooked left, not that they never touched it again. Within 10 years, 37% were free. Men got free less often than women.

pages.timelineNote: Withdrawal is well measured for alcohol. Many people get less than this.

milestones.text: Shaky, sweaty, anxious, can’t sleep. Withdrawal starts.
If you drank heavily every day, seizure risk peaks here (8–48 hours). Don’t do these days alone.
Confusion or seeing things is an emergency (the DTs). Call for help.
You feel better, and the thought comes: “maybe it wasn’t that bad.”
The low mood lifts for most. In 191 men, depression fell from 42% to 6%.
A Friday, a bar or old friends can still set off a strong pull, even at day 60. Expected. It doesn’t mean you’re sliding back.
Falling asleep is back to normal. Deep sleep keeps improving for 1–2 years.

beliefs.current: I need a drink to unwind after work.
beliefs.new: Drinking doesn’t take my stress away. It takes my sleep, and sleep is what would.
beliefs.proof: In sleep-lab studies, heavy drinkers who stopped needed 5–9 months before they fell asleep normally again.

beliefs.current: I only drink beer and wine, not the hard stuff.
beliefs.new: A beer, a glass of wine and a shot are the same drink to my body.
beliefs.proof: Each holds about 14 grams of pure alcohol. The body counts the alcohol, not the bottle.

beliefs.current: I’m not an alcoholic. It’s not that bad.
beliefs.new: I don’t need a label to decide I want more from life than this.
beliefs.proof: 9 in 10 Americans who drink too much, mostly binge drinkers, weren’t dependent. Harm doesn’t wait for a diagnosis: WHO says no amount is risk-free.

beliefs.current: I’ve been drinking for years. I’m stuck with it.
beliefs.new: Most people hooked on alcohol get free in the end. I’m doing it now.
beliefs.proof: In a big US survey, 90.6% of people ever hooked on alcohol are projected to get free in their lifetime; half within about 14 years.

beliefs.current: Day 4, I feel fine. Maybe it wasn’t that bad.
beliefs.new: Feeling better is the quitting working, not proof I never had to.
beliefs.proof: A Friday or a bar can still set off a strong pull at day 60, long after the body feels fine.

beliefs.current: If I can’t quit forever, why bother?
beliefs.new: Every day I keep my promise is a complete win in itself.
beliefs.proof: Total abstinence isn’t the only road: across 22 studies, cutting down worked as a goal for many, especially with support.

beliefs.current: I’ll just stop on my own this weekend.
beliefs.new: If I drink heavily every day, I stop with a doctor, not alone on a Saturday.
beliefs.proof: Withdrawal seizures cluster 8–48 hours after the last drink. Most people can withdraw at home, with medication and someone checking in.

numbers.text: of Americans who drink too much, mostly by binging, aren’t dependent.
For every 12 people who take acamprosate, one is kept from drinking again.
deaths worldwide were caused by alcohol in 2019.

footer.text: Drinking heavily every day? Talk to a doctor before you stop: seizures can come 8–48 hours after the last drink.

windows.label: Shaky, sweaty, anxious, bad sleep
windows.when: 6–36 hours

windows.label: Seizure risk, if you drank heavily every day
windows.when: 8–48 hours, highest around hour 24

windows.label: Confusion, seeing things (the DTs)
windows.when: Day 2–7, rare

windows.label: Irritable, anxious, poor sleep
windows.when: Day 5 to several weeks

windows.label: Fridays, bars, old friends still pull
windows.when: Week 1 to day 60, the last check

windows.label: Less pleasure in things
windows.when: Seen in some people up to a year

windows.label: Light, broken sleep, slowly mending
windows.when: Falling asleep normal by month 5–9; full repair 1–2 years

do: Write down what drinking does for you: unwinding, sleep, confidence, fun with friends.
Each one is a belief to test. Start with the table above.
Unwinding: a walk, a shower, a hard workout, a show.
Going out: an alcohol-free beer in your hand, ordered first, before anyone asks.
Friends: see the ones you’d enjoy sober; meet them for food, sport or coffee.
Clear the house of drink the day before.
Tell one person the date.
Plan every Friday for the first two months. That’s where the pull lives.

proof.text: A Friday, a bar or old friends can still set off a strong pull at day 60.

do: When “just one” comes, answer the way a non-drinker would: “I don’t drink.”
Count the mornings you wake up clear, not the days you missed.
Ask a doctor about acamprosate or naltrexone.
Try AA or another group that meets weekly.
Drinking heavily every day? See a doctor before you stop.

proof.text: For every 12 people who take acamprosate, one is kept from drinking again. In a Cochrane review, AA beat other treatments for staying sober.

pages.title: Quitting nicotine

hero.line: of people ever hooked on nicotine are expected to get free of it in their lifetime.
hero.sub: Half took about 26 years. You don’t have to wait that long.
hero.basedOn: A US survey of 43,093 adults in 2001–02. 6,937 of them had ever been hooked on nicotine. From the age each one got free, a standard statistical model projects the share over a whole life.
hero.caveat: “Free” means no signs of being hooked left, not that they never touched it again. Within 10 years, 18% were free. Men got free less often than women.

pages.timelineNote: Measured in smokers. Vape-only and pouch-only quitters have not been timed.

milestones.text: Irritable, restless, can’t focus. The first week is the worst of it.
Most relapses happen here.
One puff matters: 83–97% of patch users who smoked at all in week 2 were smoking again at 6 months.
The withdrawal fades out.
Withdrawal has faded, yet a coffee, a drink or a break can still bring a strong urge. Expected. It doesn’t mean you’re sliding back.
Most of any weight gain has happened: 4–5 kg on average by a year; 16% lose weight.
Less anxiety, depression and stress than people who kept smoking. An urge can still pop up; it’s strong for about 1 in 10.

beliefs.current: A cigarette is the only thing that calms me down.
beliefs.new: Smoking creates the stress it seems to relieve. Quitting is what calms me down.
beliefs.proof: Across 26 studies, people who quit had less anxiety, depression and stress than people who kept smoking: as big a change as antidepressants give.

beliefs.current: I enjoy it. I don’t want to give it up.
beliefs.new: Much of the enjoyment is relief from an itch nicotine gave me. The itch is gone within a month.
beliefs.proof: The irritability, anxiety and restlessness between doses peak in the first week off and fade over 2–4 weeks.

beliefs.current: Smoking keeps my weight down.
beliefs.new: A few kilos is a fair trade, and I can handle them.
beliefs.proof: Average gain is 4–5 kg after a year, mostly in the first 3 months. 16% of quitters lose weight.

beliefs.current: I’ve smoked too long. It’s too late.
beliefs.new: Most people hooked on nicotine get free in the end. I’m not waiting 26 years.
beliefs.proof: In a big US survey, 83.7% of people ever hooked on nicotine are projected to get free in their lifetime; half took about 26 years.

beliefs.current: Just one won’t hurt. I’m still quit.
beliefs.new: There’s no “just one”. One is how quit turns into smoking again.
beliefs.proof: Among patch users who smoked at all in week 2, 83–97% were smoking again at 6 months.

beliefs.current: Vapes and pouches are basically harmless.
beliefs.new: Switching is a step down, not a way out.
beliefs.proof: Vaping exposes you to far fewer toxicants than smoking, but it hooks you too, more at higher strengths. 6–8 mg pouches deliver nicotine like snuff.

beliefs.current: Patches are cheating. Cold turkey or nothing.
beliefs.new: I’ll take whatever doubles my chances. Pride doesn’t quit for me.
beliefs.proof: Only 3–5% of unaided attempts last 6–12 months. Varenicline makes you more than twice as likely to quit (41 trials).

numbers.text: of quit attempts made without any help last 6–12 months.
as likely to quit with varenicline, across 41 trials and 17,395 people.
average weight gain a year after quitting. 16% lose weight.

windows.label: Irritable, restless, can’t focus, poor sleep
windows.when: Worst in week 1, gone by week 2–4

windows.label: Coffee, a drink, a break still pull
windows.when: Week 1 to day 35, the last check

windows.label: Weight goes up, most of it by month 3
windows.when: 4–5 kg by a year on average; 16% lose weight

windows.label: An odd urge, years later
windows.when: Years 1–10; strong for about 1 in 10

do: Write down what you think nicotine gives you: calm, focus, a break.
Most of it is relief from the itch nicotine itself made. Test each one in the table above.
Breaks: step outside anyway, without it. Walk, drink water.
Coffee: change the place or the time for the first weeks.
Hands and mouth: gum, a toothpick, seeds.
Throw out every pack, vape and pouch the night before.
Treat week 2 as the test: not one puff.

proof.text: Most relapses happen in the first 8 days. Of patch users who smoked at all in week 2, 83–97% were smoking again at 6 months.

do: Say “I don’t smoke”, not “I’m trying to quit”.
When the urge comes with coffee or a drink, it’s the habit asking, not your body.
Ask a doctor about varenicline.
Or use a patch plus gum or lozenge, not just one.
Still on cigarettes? A vape helps more smokers stop than patches do. It’s a switch, not an exit.

proof.text: With varenicline, more than twice as many people quit (41 trials, 17,395 people). Patch plus a second form beats one form.

pages.title: Quitting weed

hero.line: of people ever hooked on weed are expected to get free of it in their lifetime.
hero.sub: Half within about 6 years. You don’t have to wait that long.
hero.basedOn: A US survey of 43,093 adults in 2001–02. 530 of them had ever been hooked on weed. From the age each one got free, a standard statistical model projects the share over a whole life.
hero.caveat: “Free” means no signs of being hooked left, not that they never touched it again. Within 10 years, 66% were free. Men got free less often than women.

pages.timelineNote: From small studies (18 and 67 people). Many people get less than this.

milestones.text: Sleep goes first: insomnia is at its worst on day 1.
Most symptoms peak: irritable, anxious, restless, no appetite.
“Now I can finally handle it.” The moderation thought shows up.
Vivid, strange dreams peak. Normal.
Most of the withdrawal is behind you.
Your brain’s cannabis receptors are back to normal.
Sleep and dreams can still be off. It passes.
The moderation thought comes back.

beliefs.current: Weed isn’t addictive.
beliefs.new: If it weren’t, I wouldn’t be reading this.
beliefs.proof: About 3 in 10 US users had a cannabis use disorder in 2012–13, and 47% of regular users get withdrawal when they stop.

beliefs.current: Weed is the only thing that gets me to sleep.
beliefs.new: Weed knocks me out. It doesn’t give me good sleep. A few rough nights buy my real sleep back.
beliefs.proof: THC may help you fall asleep faster but harm sleep quality over time. Quitting insomnia is worst on day 1 and eases over weeks.

beliefs.current: It’s natural, so it’s harmless.
beliefs.new: Natural isn’t the same as safe. Daily strong weed messes with my head.
beliefs.proof: Daily use of high-potency cannabis: 4.8 times the odds of a first psychotic disorder (11 European sites).

beliefs.current: Day 10, I feel fine. Now I can handle it.
beliefs.new: Feeling fine means the withdrawal is over, not that I’m in control again.
beliefs.proof: Brain receptors recover in about 4 weeks, but the moderation thought shows up around day 10 and month 2 in quitters’ own accounts.

beliefs.current: I’ve smoked for years. I’m stuck.
beliefs.new: 97% of people hooked on weed are expected to get free. I’m next.
beliefs.proof: In a big US survey, 97.2% of people ever hooked on weed are projected to get free in their lifetime; half within about 6 years.

beliefs.current: Nothing’s fun without it. This flatness is forever.
beliefs.new: The flatness is temporary. It fades the longer I stay off.
beliefs.proof: Across 32 studies, loss of pleasure followed heavy use and faded with abstinence. No study has tracked it month by month for weed.

beliefs.current: These crazy dreams mean something’s wrong.
beliefs.new: The wild dreams are part of coming off. They pass.
beliefs.proof: Vivid, strange dreams peak around days 9–11 and can last past day 45.

numbers.text: of regular users get withdrawal when they stop (47 studies).
is when most symptoms peak. Most are gone by day 14.
the odds of psychosis with daily high-potency weed.

stages.text: Cravings, then no appetite and an upset stomach. Many say they are starting over after earlier tries.
Cravings, stomach trouble, no sleep and anxiety. Vivid dreams start to show up.
Cravings, anxiety and low mood lead. Stomach trouble starts to fade.
Cravings, anxiety, low mood, a short temper. Tiredness shows up.
Cravings and low mood lead. Sleep complaints drop. New: feeling flat, nothing is fun.
Cravings and low mood. New: missing weed and making it sound better than it was, and brain fog.
Cravings and low mood still lead. New: boredom and empty time, and the “one won’t hurt” thought.

community.note: Cravings are the top topic at every stage. That doesn’t mean they grow: people who are doing fine mostly stop posting, so the later stages are written mostly by people who still struggle.
community.relapse: 103 of the 221 relapse posts with a day count (47%) came after more than a month off. The reasons named most: “just a little won’t hurt” or “I can moderate now”; withdrawal got too hard; friends, a party, or a partner who smokes.

windows.label: No appetite, upset stomach, shaky
windows.when: Day 1–14, worst on day 2–6

windows.label: Irritable, angry, anxious, restless
windows.when: Day 1–14, worst on day 2–6

windows.label: Can’t sleep
windows.when: Worst on day 1; can last past day 45

windows.label: Vivid, strange dreams
windows.when: Worst around day 9–11; can last past day 45

do: Write down what weed does for you: sleep, boredom, anxiety, fun.
Each one is a belief to test. Start with the table above.
Sleep: same wake-up time every day, no screens in bed.
Evenings: plan the first 14 in advance: gym, cooking, a friend, a game.
Anxiety: a walk or a hard workout when it spikes.
Throw out the stash, grinder and papers. Delete the dealer’s number.
Expect the first two weeks to be the hardest.

proof.text: Most symptoms peak on days 2–6 and are mostly gone by day 14. “Now I can handle it” tends to show up around day 10 and again at month 2.

do: When someone offers, say “I don’t smoke”, not “I’m taking a break”.
Notice the “I can moderate now” thought, and treat it as a symptom.
Look for CBT with motivation sessions, over a month or more.
Ask about programmes that reward clean tests.

proof.text: In a Cochrane review of 23 trials, therapy made people about 2.5 times as likely to be off weed at the end (low-quality evidence).

pages.title: Quitting cocaine

hero.line: of people ever hooked on cocaine are expected to get free of it in their lifetime.
hero.sub: Half within about 5 years. You don’t have to wait that long.
hero.basedOn: A US survey of 43,093 adults in 2001–02. 408 of them had ever been hooked on cocaine. From the age each one got free, a standard statistical model projects the share over a whole life.
hero.caveat: “Free” means no signs of being hooked left, not that they never touched it again. Within 10 years, 76% were free. Men got free less often than women.

pages.timelineNote: Coke has no classic withdrawal. Timed in small studies only.

milestones.text: The crash: heavy sleep and irritability.
Dark thoughts can spike. If they do, tell someone tonight.
Low mood and craving ease bit by bit.
You feel rested, but measured sleep is at its worst.
The craving you feel keeps getting weaker. The people, places and things around coke can still hit hard.

beliefs.current: Coke isn’t really addictive. There’s no real withdrawal.
beliefs.new: No shakes doesn’t mean no hook. The pull lives in my head, for months.
beliefs.proof: Coke withdrawal is mostly mood and sleep, not sickness. But the brain’s reaction to coke cues stays high for months.

beliefs.current: The craving’s gone, so I’m safe.
beliefs.new: Feeling less pull isn’t the same as being safe. People, places and things can still hit hard in months 1–6.
beliefs.proof: In 76 users, the brain’s response to cocaine cues was higher at 1 and 6 months than at 1 week, while felt craving fell.

beliefs.current: It’s just a party drug.
beliefs.new: Coke plus drink is a heart risk, not a party.
beliefs.proof: Together they form cocaethylene, linked to an 18–25 times higher risk of sudden death. Street stimulants can also contain fentanyl.

beliefs.current: I’ll never get out of this.
beliefs.new: 99% of people hooked on coke are expected to get free. Mine starts now.
beliefs.proof: In a big US survey, 99.2% of people ever hooked on cocaine are projected to get free in their lifetime; half within about 5 years.

beliefs.current: I’m sleeping great now. I’m fine.
beliefs.new: Feeling rested isn’t proof. My sleep is still healing.
beliefs.proof: In a sleep-lab study of 12 users, measured sleep was worst at days 14–17, while they rated it at its best.

numbers.text: the odds of staying off at 12 weeks with rewards for clean tests plus community support.
higher risk of sudden death when coke is mixed with alcohol.
sleep is at its worst while it feels best.

footer.text: Dark thoughts in the crash are common and they pass. If they don’t, talk to someone tonight.

windows.label: The crash: heavy sleep, irritable
windows.when: First 12–24 hours

windows.label: Low mood
windows.when: Worst at the start, eases over 4 weeks

windows.label: The craving you feel
windows.when: Worst in the first days, keeps falling to a year

windows.label: Sleep worse, though it feels better
windows.when: Weeks 1–7, worst on day 14–17

windows.label: People, places, things still pull
windows.when: Can hit hard from month 1 to 6; lower by a year

do: Write down what coke gives you: confidence, energy, the night going on.
Each one is a belief to test. Start with the table above.
Nights out: go with people who don’t use, and leave before the hour it usually comes out.
If drinking is how coke starts for you, plan the drinking too.
Energy: sleep, food, training. The crash is borrowed energy paid back.
Block and delete the dealer before the date.
Expect a crash the first day: heavy sleep, low mood. It passes.

proof.text: The crash brings 12–24 hours of heavy sleep and irritability.

do: In months 1–6, when the pull comes, name it: a trigger, not a need.
Say “I don’t do coke” when it’s offered.

proof.text: Felt craving falls, but cues can still hit hard in months 1–6.

do: Ask for a programme that rewards clean tests (contingency management).
There’s no approved pill for this; the right therapy is the standard.

proof.text: Rewards for clean tests plus community support: 7.6 times the odds of staying off at 12 weeks (50 trials).

pages.title: Quitting porn

hero.sub: A randomised trial of 176 regular users. Stopping is safe to try.

pages.timelineNote: Science has measured only the first week. Forum data could fill in the rest.

milestones.text: No withdrawal: regular users who stopped for a week had none, compared with people who kept watching.
If you watched daily and felt hooked, craving may rise a little (an early finding).
About 1 in 3 reboot journals describe a low-desire “flatline”. Nobody has measured when it starts or how long it lasts.

beliefs.current: Everyone watches it. It’s harmless.
beliefs.new: Normal isn’t the bar. I decide what it costs me.
beliefs.proof: 91.5% of men in one US online sample watched in the past month; about 11% of US men agree “I am addicted to pornography”.

beliefs.current: Quitting means a brutal flatline and weeks of withdrawal.
beliefs.new: A week off costs me nothing. There’s no measured withdrawal.
beliefs.proof: In a randomised trial of 176 regular users, those who stopped for 7 days had no withdrawal symptoms compared with those who kept watching.

beliefs.current: Staying off it will give me superpowers.
beliefs.new: Quitting won’t make me magnetic. Going out and talking to women will.
beliefs.proof: No study shows abstinence gives special energy or pull. Wanting to abstain tracked attitudes and religiosity, not anything people actually did.

beliefs.current: Porn wrecked my erections.
beliefs.new: If my erections are off, I get checked, and I don’t blame porn alone.
beliefs.proof: Across three samples, simply using porn wasn’t consistently linked to erection problems, and over a year it predicted no change.

beliefs.current: I must be an addict. Look how bad I feel about it.
beliefs.new: Guilt isn’t a measure. I judge porn by what it costs me, not by how ashamed I feel.
beliefs.proof: Over a year, moral disapproval predicted feeling addicted (r = 0.46 and 0.61); how much people watched barely did (r = 0.13 and 0.11).

beliefs.current: Blockers never work for me.
beliefs.new: Blockers work when someone else holds the password.
beliefs.proof: From quitters’ accounts, not trials: blockers “work only when someone else holds the key”.

numbers.text: of men in one US sample watched porn in the past month.
of US men say “I am addicted to pornography”.
drop in viewing with 12 sessions of ACT therapy, against 21% on the waitlist (28 men).

do: Write down what porn does for you: stress relief, sleep, boredom, loneliness.
Each one is a belief to test. Start with the table above.
Late nights: the phone charges outside the bedroom.
Stress or boredom: a walk, a workout, a call with a friend.
Loneliness: put that energy into meeting real people.
Install a blocker and give the password to someone else.
Start with a 7-day break as an experiment.

proof.text: In a trial of 176 regular users, a week off caused no withdrawal. People who quit say blockers work only when someone else holds the key.

do: If shame is the engine, work on your values, not only the habit.
A slip is information, not proof you’re broken.

proof.text: Feeling “addicted” tracks the clash with your own values more than how much you watch.

do: Look for a therapist who uses CBT or ACT.

proof.text: In one small trial (28 men), viewing fell 93% after 12 sessions of ACT, against 21% on the waiting list.

pages.title: Quitting betting

hero.line: of people who quit gambling bet again at least once in their first year.
hero.sub: A slip is normal. What you do the next day counts.

pages.timelineNote: No withdrawal clock has been measured for gambling. These are the moments that matter.

milestones.text: 1 in 4 felt restless or irritable; 41% felt anger, guilt or disappointment. Nobody has timed it.
The classic slip: a good mood, an evening, alone, thinking about money.
Only 8% had no gambling at all in their first year. Expect a slip; plan the next day.

beliefs.current: If I keep going, I’ll win it back.
beliefs.new: The money is gone. Chasing it is the problem talking.
beliefs.proof: Chasing losses is a core symptom of gambling disorder. Thoughts of winning and needing money were the top reasons for major relapses.

beliefs.current: I know football. It’s skill, not luck.
beliefs.new: Feeling skilled is part of the trap, not a way out of it.
beliefs.proof: Researchers who studied 30 expert hockey bettors concluded their “skills” were thinking errors. Believing you can predict outcomes is a measured gambling distortion.

beliefs.current: So close. I’m due a win.
beliefs.new: A near miss is a loss. My brain just lights it up like a win.
beliefs.proof: In a brain-scan study, near-misses felt worse than losses but raised the urge to play and lit up the same reward areas as real wins.

beliefs.current: Three months clean. A hundred for fun won’t hurt.
beliefs.new: A good mood is exactly when I’m most likely to slip.
beliefs.proof: Relapses followed good moods as often as bad ones, most often in the evening, alone, thinking about money.

beliefs.current: Self-exclusion is pointless. I’ll find a way anyway.
beliefs.new: Every block I set up is a wall between me and my worst night.
beliefs.proof: People do break exclusions (8–59%). Still, across 19 studies, problem gambling fell from 61–95% of people before exclusion to 13–26% after.

beliefs.current: I can handle my own money.
beliefs.new: Someone I trust holds my money for a while. That’s a strategy, not a weakness.
beliefs.proof: UK guidance lists a family member controlling the finances; people who quit rank handing money over above any blocking app.

numbers.text: problem gambling before and after self-exclusion (19 studies).
felt restless or irritable when cutting down.
CBT cut symptoms and money lost for the first 3 months after therapy. Longer is unknown.

footer.text: Losses can bring dark thoughts, even if you’ve never had them before. If they come, talk to someone tonight.

do: Write down what betting gives you: excitement, a shot at fixing money, something riding on the game.
Each one is a belief to test. Start with the table above.
Match days: watch with friends, no betting app on the phone.
Money worry: a plan with real numbers instead of a win.
The buzz: sport you play, not sport you bet on.
Self-exclude from every site, turn on your bank’s gambling block, and hand card control to someone you trust.
Plan the day after a slip now, before it happens.

proof.text: 92% bet again at least once in their first year. What you do the next day counts.

do: Say “I don’t bet” when the group bet starts.
When you think about a loss, don’t chase it. That money is gone either way.
Look for gambling-focused CBT.
Bring in a partner or family member, if you both agree.
Gamblers Anonymous for people who’ve been there.

proof.text: In a Cochrane review of 14 trials, CBT cut symptoms and money lost in the first 3 months after therapy.

pages.title: Cutting down: phone and social media

hero.line: of the time on social apps, browsers and YouTube is down to self-control problems, economists estimate.
hero.sub: That’s the part you never chose. Take it back.

pages.timelineNote: Studies of breaks, not of quitting. The science disagrees on mood.

milestones.text: You’ll want it. Craving rises; mood and anxiety don’t.
Breaks shorter than a week can leave mood slightly worse. Don’t judge it on day 3.
A week or longer: mood slightly better on average (one pooled review; another found no effect).
Four weeks off Facebook: people were happier, and used it less afterwards.

beliefs.current: I’ll just check one thing.
beliefs.new: “One thing” is how I lose an hour. I plan my checks; I don’t trust the moment.
beliefs.proof: Economists estimated self-control problems drive 31% of social media use, and people partly underestimate their own.

beliefs.current: Without my phone I’ll be anxious and miserable.
beliefs.new: A day off makes me want it. A week off makes me feel better.
beliefs.proof: A 24-hour break raised craving but not anxiety or low mood. Breaks of a week or more left mood slightly better on average.

beliefs.current: Everyone’s on it. It’s just normal life now.
beliefs.new: Being on it is normal. Being run by it isn’t.
beliefs.proof: Addiction-level use is a minority: 5% under strict criteria, 25% under loose ones, across 32 nations.

beliefs.current: Limits never work for me.
beliefs.new: Limits I set in advance work. Willpower in the moment doesn’t.
beliefs.proof: In a randomised experiment, letting people set their own future screen-time limits substantially cut use.

beliefs.current: If I log off, I’ll miss out.
beliefs.new: What I miss on the feed, I get back in my life.
beliefs.proof: Four weeks off Facebook raised well-being, and people used it less afterwards.

proof.text: In a large experiment, limits people set themselves cut use a lot. Breaks under a week can leave mood slightly worse; a week or more, slightly better.

pages.title: Cutting down: binge eating and sugar

hero.line: of adults score as hooked on food on a standard questionnaire.
hero.sub: The pull is mostly junk that mixes sugar and fat, not sugar alone.

pages.timelineNote: Only the first two weeks have been studied, and the two studies disagree.

milestones.text: People remember days 2–5 as the hardest: cravings, irritability, low mood.
In a trial of 107 people, cutting ultra-processed food caused no more withdrawal than an ordinary diet.
Skipping meals to make up for it sets up the next binge.

beliefs.current: I’m addicted to sugar. One bite and I’m gone.
beliefs.new: Sugar isn’t a drug. Junk that mixes sugar and fat is the one to watch.
beliefs.proof: There’s little human evidence that sugar itself is addictive. The strongest signal is for processed foods that combine refined carbs and fat.

beliefs.current: Cutting junk food will feel like coming off drugs.
beliefs.new: A couple of rough days, not a detox.
beliefs.proof: People recall days 2–5 as hardest, but in a trial of 107 people, cutting ultra-processed food caused no more withdrawal than an ordinary diet.

beliefs.current: I binge because I’ve got no willpower.
beliefs.new: Bingeing is a known, treatable pattern, not a character flaw.
beliefs.proof: Binge-eating disorder affects 2.0% of US men in their lifetime. Talking therapy, mostly CBT, has large effects on binges in trials.

beliefs.current: I’ll make up for it by not eating tomorrow.
beliefs.new: Skipping meals sets up the next binge. I eat regular meals.
beliefs.proof: In a 5-year study of 496 girls, fasting predicted later binge eating. Not yet tested in adult men.

beliefs.current: I’ve been good for weeks. One slice will ruin it.
beliefs.new: Food isn’t all or nothing. A slice at a party is fine; the strict rule is what breaks.
beliefs.proof: You can’t stop eating, so some moderation is unavoidable, and extreme restriction predicted later bingeing.

Evenings: a planned snack you actually enjoy, not nothing.
Stress: a walk before the kitchen.
Reward: something that isn’t food, planned in advance.
Keep your trigger foods out of the house for the three months.

proof.text: Skipping meals to make up for a binge sets up the next one (in studies of teenage girls; not tested in men).

do: Not “I’m on a diet”. “I eat real food.”
One binge is one meal, not a ruined week.
Try a CBT-based self-help book or programme.
If it keeps happening, see a doctor or a CBT therapist.

proof.text: Across 81 trials, CBT and CBT self-help beat waiting, and some medicines helped a little (low-quality evidence).
